```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

Two short worked examples. Both run on the package's bundled `earnings_panel`
(a synthetic, CPS-style two-wave panel of 7,600 women, 1982–2020; see
`?earnings_panel`) and aim to show the package's two main modes — descriptive
and causal — without doing a full analysis.

* [Example 1: Descriptive within/between decomposition](#e1)
* [Example 2: Causal decomposition — the motherhood penalty](#e2)

```{r setup, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(ineqx)
data("earnings_panel")
```

---

### Example 1: Descriptive within/between decomposition {#e1}

Women in `earnings_panel` are grouped into low/middle/high socioeconomic
status (`ses`). We ask: how much earnings inequality lies *within* each SES
tier vs *between* tiers, and how has that changed since 1982? For a clean
annual cross-section we use each woman's first wave (`post == 0`).

```{r, message = FALSE}
desc <- ineqx(
  y = "earnweek", ystat = "CV2",
  group = "ses",
  time = "year", ref = 1982,
  weights = "earnwt",
  data = subset(earnings_panel, post == 0)
)
```

We use `ystat = "CV2"` (squared coefficient of variation, $\sigma^2/\mu^2$)
rather than `"Var"` so that the high-income tier doesn't mechanically dominate
the decomposition. `"VL"` (variance of logs) is also accepted but is generally
not recommended — see the FAQ.

```{r}
print(desc)
```

Within- vs between-group inequality over time:

```{r fig1, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4, out.width = "85%", dpi = 150, fig.align = "center"}
plot(desc, type = "wibe")
```

Decomposition of the change since 1982 into contributions from changing means
($\Delta_\mu$), changing dispersions ($\Delta_\sigma$), and changing group
shares ($\Delta_\pi$):

```{r fig2, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4, out.width = "85%", dpi = 150, fig.align = "center"}
plot(desc, type = "decomp")
```

$CV^2$ rises from about 0.8 in 1982 to about 1.2 in 2019, and almost all of
that inequality — and its growth — lies *within* SES tiers. The increase
traces to growing within-group dispersion ($\Delta_\sigma$), partly offset by
rising mean earnings ($\Delta_\mu$), which lower $CV^2$ for a given standard
deviation. Shifts in the SES composition ($\Delta_\pi$) play almost no role.
This is the basic motivation for taking within-group inequality seriously.

---

### Example 2: Causal decomposition — the motherhood penalty {#e2}

Same dataset, now asking a causal question: how does motherhood affect
earnings inequality among women, and how has that effect changed?

We restrict the sample to women with positive earnings and fit a
difference-in-differences model (treatment = `mother`, post-period = `post`)
with education-by-decade interactions for both the mean and log-SD of
earnings. GAMLSS does the heavy lifting internally. For `ystat = "CV2"`, keep
the outcome in levels and use `post` for the DiD contrast; applying `CV2` to
first-differenced outcomes is not recommended.

```{r, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
df <- subset(earnings_panel, earnweek > 0)

causal <- ineqx(
  y = "earnweek", ystat = "CV2",
  treat = "mother", post = "post",
  group = "educ",
  time = "decade", ref = 1980,
  formula_mu    = ~ mother * post * educ * factor(decade) + age,
  formula_sigma = ~ mother * post * educ * factor(decade),
  weights = "earnwt",
  se = "delta",
  data = df
)
```

#### Cross-sectional split: het and cov sub-components

The treatment effect on inequality at each time decomposes into
$\tau_B = \text{het}_B + \text{cov}_B$ (between groups) and
$\tau_W = \text{het}_W + \text{cov}_W$ (within groups). See the [Model
structure](model.html) page for the exact formulas. `plot(..., type = "wibe",
stats = ...)` shows all four series at once:

```{r fig3, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.5, out.width = "90%", dpi = 150, fig.align = "center", message = FALSE}
plot(causal, type = "wibe",
     stats = c("het_b", "cov_b", "het_w", "cov_w"),
     ci = TRUE)
```

The dominant series here is **`het_W`** — the within-group component driven
by the average treatment effect on log-SD ($\bar\lambda$). It is positive and
large: motherhood widens within-education earnings dispersion, though less so
in later decades. The within-group **`cov_W`** term is negative and the
between-group **`cov_B`** term (sorting of mean effects $\beta$ across
education groups) is small and positive: the motherhood penalty is largest in
the lowest-earning education group, which widens between-group gaps. Note
this is exactly the kind of pattern that mean-based methods miss.

#### Longitudinal: behavioral / compositional / pre-treatment

How has the motherhood effect's contribution to inequality *changed* since
1980? `type = "shapley"` displays the three-channel decomposition with the
range across the six possible orderings:

```{r fig4, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.5, out.width = "90%", dpi = 150, fig.align = "center", message = FALSE}
plot(causal, type = "shapley")
```

The **behavioral** channel ($\Delta_\beta + \Delta_\lambda$, how
motherhood's per-group effects have changed) is the largest and negative —
the motherhood penalties on both the mean and the dispersion of earnings have
shrunk since 1980, so motherhood adds less to inequality than it used to. The
**compositional** channel ($\Delta_\pi$) is also negative: the share of women
who become mothers has fallen. **Pre-treatment** shifts ($\Delta_\mu +
\Delta_\sigma$, changes in baseline inequality) push in the opposite
direction: because baseline earnings have become more unequal, the same
treatment effects now contribute more to inequality.

A more thorough analysis would add controls for race, marital status, and
age splines; would model the pre-trends formally; and would use
bootstrap rather than delta-method SEs. See `?ineqx`, `?boot_config`, and the
[Tutorial](tutorial.html) for the full toolbox.
